title: What Made Work Feel Good
text:
In the late 1950s the psychologist Frederick Herzberg and his colleagues interviewed about two hundred engineers and accountants working for companies around Pittsburgh. They asked each person to describe a time when they had felt exceptionally good about their job, and a time when they had felt exceptionally bad, and then to explain what had caused those feelings.

The answers fell into two different groups. The good times were mostly about the work itself: achieving something, being recognized for it, doing interesting work, being given responsibility and having a chance to grow. The bad times were mostly about the surroundings of the work: company policy and administration, supervision, relationships, working conditions and pay.

From this, Herzberg built his two-factor theory. He called the second group "hygiene" factors: when they were poor, people were unhappy, but fixing them only removed the unhappiness. The first group he called motivators, because they were what actually moved people to put in more effort and feel satisfied. He later summed up the argument in a widely read Harvard Business Review article in 1968.
lesson: Fair pay and decent conditions prevent misery, but they rarely inspire. To motivate people, give them meaningful work, responsibility and real recognition.
people: Frederick Herzberg, Bernard Mausner, Barbara Snyderman
source: Herzberg, F., Mausner, B., and Snyderman, B. B. (1959). The Motivation to Work. Wiley.
caveat: Later studies using other methods often failed to find two clean factors; people may credit themselves for good times and blame circumstances for bad ones.
